column2: Oh, I wish for his life; such a man does not deserve to be killed. Good men who do not flee in battle are very hard to find.
That man has done me an ill, by whom he was slain in battle—saying this aloud, he should honour the slayers when in private.
For the slayers and the slain alike, whatever the offenders do, he should cry out with raised arm, wishing to win the people.
Thus in all conditions, acting with conciliation first, a king who knows dharma and is free from fear becomes dear to beings.
And all beings place trust in him, Bharata; one who is trusted can be enjoyed at will when he comes near.
Therefore a king should inspire trust in all beings without deceit, and guard the earth on every side, he who wishes to enjoy it.
[Bhishma said:] "On this too they recite this ancient history, Yudhishthira: the conversation of Brihaspati and Indra.
Having saluted Brihaspati with joined palms, the lord of the gods, slayer of heroes, Vasava, approached and asked:

Brahmana, how should I deal with my enemies, ever alert, and restrain them by means without uprooting them?

Then Brihaspati, skilled in dharma, wealth and desire, quick of wit, and knowing the rules of kingship, replied to Purandara:

One should never wish to restrain wrongdoers by quarrel; that is the way of children, that impatience and want of forbearance. An enemy should not be exposed by one who wishes his destruction.

[Indra said:] "What are the signs of a wicked man, best of Brahmanas? How should one know the wicked? Asked this, tell me."
[Brihaspati said:] "He speaks of faults behind one's back, resents good qualities, and when others are praised he is silent and turned away.
In silence too, if knowledge is not the cause, there are trust, biting the lip, and shaking the head.
He is constantly in contact and speaks when apart; he changes when unseen, and on seeing does not speak.
He comes apart and eats separately, not properly as now; in seat, bed and vehicle his feelings are to be marked especially.
Distress in the distressed and joy in the beloved—this much is the mark of a friend; the opposite is to be understood as the mark of an enemy.
You should understand these as thus stated, lord of the Thirty; the nature of thoroughly wicked men is stronger.
Thus the recognition of the wicked has been told to you, best of gods." Considering the true meaning of the science as it should be, the lord of the immortals...
[Bhishma said:] "Devoted to destroying his enemies, he did Brihaspati's words unfailingly; the foe-slayer Purandara moved in time for victory and brought his enemies under his power."
[Bhishma said:] "Here this history of Kshemadarshin is recited; I shall tell you that; hear it, Yudhishthira.
We have heard that the sage Kalakavrikshiya once came to the king's son Kshemadarshin, whose strength had waned; he, fallen into hard calamity, embraced his feet and asked:

A man who has a share in wealth, striving again and again and not obtaining a kingdom, such as I—what should he do, Brahmana?
mahabharata:12:105.5	Other than death, other than theft, other than taking refuge, other than petty conduct—tell me that, best of the good.
mahabharata:12:105.6	For one afflicted by disease, of mind or otherwise, a learned and wise man like you would be the means.
mahabharata:12:105.7	A man who has turned from desires, restraining them, prospers in happiness, abandoning joy and sorrow and gaining wealth that is joyless.
mahabharata:12:105.8	I grieve for those whose happiness depends on wealth; for my own many riches are lost, come like a dream.

Thus addressed by the wise prince of Kosala, the sage Kalakavrikshiya of great splendour replied:

This understanding you should have had before, knowing that all this is impermanent, and I and what is mine.
mahabharata:12:105.13	Whatever you think exists, know that all of it does not; so the wise man is not troubled even in hard calamity.
mahabharata:12:105.14	What has been and what will be—surely that will not be; knowing thus what is to be known, you will be freed from evils.
mahabharata:12:105.15	What was in the earlier gathering and in the still earlier ones—all that is not; knowing that, who would burn with grief?
mahabharata:12:105.16	This having been, is not; and not having been, comes to be; there is no power in grief; how should a man grieve?

mahabharata:12:105.18	Seeing the impermanence of yourself, why do you grieve for them? Understand with intellect that you surely will not be.
mahabharata:12:105.19	I and you, king, and your enemies and friends, will surely not be, and everything will not be.
mahabharata:12:105.20	Those men who are twenty or thirty years old will all die before a hundred autumns.
mahabharata:12:105.21	Even if a man is released from great wealth, thinking this is not mine", he should do what is dear to himself.
Those who know that what is yet to come is not mine, what is past is not mine, and who consider fate stronger—those wise ones, they say, are in the place of the good.
Even those without wealth live and rule a kingdom; men endowed with intellect and manliness, equal to you or greater.
And they do not grieve as you do; therefore do not you grieve either. Are you not better than they, or equal in intellect and manliness?"
[The prince said:] "That kingdom of mine came by chance, I think; all this is carried off by great time, Brahmana.
For me thus carried off as by a current, ascetic, I see this fruit: that I live on what I get."
[The sage said:] "Not grieving, Kausalya, over the future and the past, by true determination—be so in all matters.
Desire aims that can be obtained, never those that cannot; enjoying what is present, do not grieve over what is to come.
As you are satisfied with what is obtained, Kausalya, so will you delight; you do not grieve though bereft of fortune, with a pure nature?
Because of earlier past states, the evil-minded one, unfortunate, ever blames the Creator and cannot bear those who have got wealth.
And he thinks others unworthy, men of fortune; for this reason this sorrow continues all the more.
Endowed with envy and excess, king, men think themselves great; are you not like that, wise one, jealous, lord of Kosala?
Bear the fortune of others, though you have none; skilled people enjoy even fortune that is elsewhere; fortune overflows even from one's enemies.
Men who follow dharma, heroes who know the dharma of renunciation, themselves give up fortune and sons and grandsons.
Seeing much that is brittle, and by the means of desire to know, others give this up, thinking it exceedingly hard to get.
You, however, though wise in appearance, grieve piteously, desiring unlovely aims, long past and troubled.
Seeking to know that understanding, give them up yourself, the unprofitable in the form of profit, and profits in the form of the unprofitable.
For some, loss of wealth is itself for their good; another, thinking that happiness endless, tests fortune.
One delighting in fortune thinks nothing else better; then, while he strives, his undertaking is ruined.
When, Kausalya, what is wished, obtained with difficulty, is lost, then the man, his sequence broken, turns from wealth.
Some men of good birth follow dharma; desiring happiness hereafter, they turn away from the worldly.
Some give up life, intent on greed for wealth; men without wealth do not count it life.
See their wretchedness, see their foolishness: in this impermanent life, through delusion, they cling to thirst for wealth.
In gathering that ends in loss, in life that ends in death, in union that ends in separation—who would set the mind on it?
Either wealth leaves the man, king, or the man leaves wealth; he must give up this; knowing that, who would burn?
The friends and riches of others also perish; see with intellect, king, the calamity of men themselves. Restrain, hold, control the senses, mind and speech.
In what is forbidden, hard to get and harmful, in rejected feelings and those that are impossible, one satisfied with wisdom and valiant, such as you, does not grieve.
Wishing little, steady, gentle, self-controlled, sharply resolved, endowed with celibacy, such as you is never bewildered.
You should not seek a wretched, skull-bearer's livelihood, cruel, wicked, painful, fit for the base.
Even living on roots and fruits, delight alone in the great forest, restrained in speech, self-gathered, full of compassion for all beings.
This befits a wise man: like an elephant with tusk and trunk, to delight alone in the forest and be content with little.
A great lake when stirred becomes clear by itself; this alone I see as happiness for one in such a state.
When fortune is impossible, king, and one is without ministers and the like, and fate is set against you, what do you think best?"

You will gain standing among all beings and a great following; then you will gain helpers, spirited, free from vice and pure.
One who abides in his own scripture, self-controlled, master of his senses, lifts himself up and pleases the people.
Honoured by him, steadfast and fortunate, having gained standing among all beings and a great following...
Birds, game animals, flavours, scents and fruits—in these very things engage him, so that the enemy himself may be ruined.
If he is to be resisted, or if he deserves to be overlooked, an enemy should never be exposed by one who desires discipline.
Dwell, supreme foe, in a land esteemed by the wise; serve with the "white crow" tricks the lowest of friends, to no purpose.
Set him to great and hard undertakings, such as damming rivers; let him be opposed by the strong.
Let his treasury be drained by costly gardens, beds and seats, by the pleasure of indulgence.
Let the praise of sacrifices and gifts be recounted to him among the Brahmanas; they will do what is dear to you and will lead him on like wolves.
Without doubt the virtuous king reaches the highest goal, attains the most meritorious place in heaven; but when the treasury is exhausted, Kausalya, he comes under his enemies' power.
One attached to both dharma and adharma will have the root of his strength and wealth cut off, and thereby enemies rejoice.
Disparage human effort for him and extol fate; one devoted to fate perishes quickly, without doubt.
Have him perform the Vishvajit sacrifice, and let him be parted from all his wealth; then let him go, his aim unaccomplished, oppressed, to the great people.
Recommend to him some shaven one who knows the dharma of renunciation; he may wish to renounce, or may go free from sickness.
By a perfected application of drugs that destroys all enemies, slay elephants, horses and men with contrivances.

[Bhishma said:] "Then the sage, calling the Videha king, said these words: "This man born in a royal family is known to me within.
A minister should be brave and endowed with intellect; see the king's fear from those two, and the joining of the kingdom; for righteous souls there is no other such refuge in the world.
This prince is self-perfected and follows the path of the good; served by you, he would take your enemies, great hosts.
If he should fight you, that is the kshatriya's own duty, wishing to win you in battle in his father's and grandfather's place.
And you too should fight him, standing in the vow of one wishing to conquer; without fighting, by my command, Videha, he is in your power.
Look therefore to dharma, giving up the unseemly adharma; you ought not abandon your own dharma from desire or treachery.
Victory is never constant, dear one, nor is defeat constant; therefore the other man should be fed and must also eat.
Both victory and defeat are seen in oneself; fear comes to those who leave nothing remaining, dear one, by leaving nothing remaining."
Thus addressed, he answered the best of Brahmana sages, having honoured and respected him and shown regard to the one worthy of honour:

As the greatly wise would speak, as the learned would speak, as one desiring the good would speak, what is fitting for both,
mahabharata:12:107.21	so have I been spoken to, and I shall do just so; this is the highest good; I have no doubt about it.
Then, calling the Kosalan, the Videha king said: "I have been conquered by you by dharma, policy and strength.
Conquered by your own qualities, best of kings, do not disregard yourself; behave as the victor.
I do not despise your intellect or your manliness; I do not despise you; behave as the victor.
Honoured as is fitting, king, you will go from my house to your own house." Then, having honoured the Brahmana, the two went to their homes trusting.
The Videha, bringing the Kosalan into his house straightaway, honoured the one worthy of honour with water for the feet, offerings and honey-mixture.
He gave him his daughter and various jewels. This is the highest dharma of kings: both victory and defeat are to be borne."
